feedback: If the learner expected the ball to stay lit, connect it to the lamp-off result: no Sun, no reflected light, no glow.
Reinforce: the Moon shines by bouncing back the Sun's light, like a brightly lit wall, not by making its own light like a lamp.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon produces no light of its own; it shines only by reflecting the Sun's light, so with no Sun there is nothing to see.
learnerActions: Put the ball where you can see its bright and dark halves.
Predict what happens to the ball if the lamp is switched off.
Switch off the lamp and observe: the ball goes dark, or only stays dimly visible from any other light leaking into the room, because it makes no light of its own.
Explain in a sentence where the Moon's glow comes from, using the word 'reflect'.
activities.title: Does the Moon make its own light?

feedback: If the shapes seem to disagree, return to the space view and check which part of the lit half is turned towards the Earth viewpoint.
activities.intendedInsight: Standing on Earth and looking up connects the Moon's orbital position directly to the shape you would actually see in the sky.
learnerActions: Using a 3D model, orbit the camera to view the Sun-Earth-Moon system from space, keeping the Moon's lit hemisphere always facing the Sun.
Drop the camera down to stand on Earth's surface and look up at the Moon for the current orbit position.
Compare the shape you see looking up with the lit half shown in the space view, and explain why they match.
activities.title: Fly to Earth's surface and look up (spatial extension)

feedback: Full understanding: the Moon reflects sunlight (always half-lit), phases are the changing amount of that lit half we see as it orbits monthly, and ordinary phases are separate from the rare lunar eclipse.

Partial: knows the Moon reflects sunlight and orbits Earth but still reaches for Earth's shadow or cannot say why the lit amount we see changes — return to the ball-and-lamp and the shadow-direction task.
Gap: attributes phases to Earth's shadow and/or thinks the Moon makes its own light — reteach reflected light and the orbit-position-to-shape mapping.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to reject the shadow explanation and give the reflected-light, viewing-angle reason shows understanding rather than only memorised phase names.
learnerActions: Answer whether this statement is right: 'The crescent happens because Earth's shadow covers part of the Moon' — then explain WHY in your own words.
Choose what causes Moon phases from options that include the Earth's-shadow idea as a tempting wrong answer, and justify your choice.
Match each orbit position to the shape seen from Earth, and put the phases in order.

Answer the probes: where does the Moon's glow come from if it makes no light? At a thin crescent, is the rest of the Moon gone or just not lit towards us? How is a lunar eclipse different from a crescent? How long is one orbit and phase cycle?
activities.title: Check and explain: two-tier phase questions
